Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for taking the time today. quick intros, i'm maya, i'll run through the business overview and then jordan will do a console + pilot sketch.
[00:10] Ravi (Lumenix CTO): thanks maya. ravi here. we'll mostly have sarah and tom ask infra and model questions. short on time so appreciate the focus.
[00:18] Sarah (Lumenix): hi all. we currently run multi-vendor endpoints — openAI for chat, anthropic for safety gating, together for some open models. we're exploring consolidating to reduce complexity.
[00:30] Jordan (Redwood SE): awesome. quick flag: we architect the parity map around API compatibility (params, streaming), model variants, and runtime ops — like prefix cache and batching.
[00:40] Tom (Lumenix): question right away — we need VPC/on-prem options for PHI. is private deployment an option? what's the path?
[00:48] Maya: yes, private is supported. we have a VPC package and an on-prem bundle for air-gapped installations. the control plane remains customer-controlled in the private offering. we'll send the KMS integration doc later.
[01:05] Ravi: ok, SAML/SSO and SOC2 - do you have certs? audits?
[01:09] Maya: we are SOC2 Type II. SAML, SCIM, RBAC supported. we'll attach cert pages.
[01:20] [Speaker 1]: (crosstalk) right right.
[01:30] Jordan: jumping to parity — so for openai style endpoints, Redwood exposes a drop-in API surface for text-generation and chat. small differences: tokenization edge cases and streaming chunk shapes, but we provide mapping helpers in the SDK.
[01:45] Sarah: can you show the mapping? we have prompt templating that assumes gpt-4o's streaming and embed flows.
[01:52] Jordan: sure, i'll share my screen and show a side-by-side.
[02:00] [02:00] Jordan (screen share): okay, here's a parity sheet: column A is current endpoint (openai/anthropic/together), B is Redwood equivalent, C is notes on prompt changes, D is example cURL. notice the streaming chunk id is different — sometimes 'delta' prefix is renamed, so small client-side adapter needed.
[02:25] Sarah: that's fine, we already have an adapter layer. any difference on stop tokens and function call behavior?
[02:32] Jordan: function-calling is supported; we emulate the openai function schema. however, for anthropic-style assistant messages, there are subtle role name changes (assistant vs system), and the safety signals are surfaced via a separate 'safety' field in the event payload. we document those.
[02:55] Ravi: throughput-wise, how do you compare to hosted openai? we care about p95 latency for 1-2k qps.
[03:03] Jordan: for hosted, we publish benchmark profiles per model. for Lumenix's expected average sequence length ~300 tokens, our benchmark for similar-size models shows median latency on par with public endpoints; and the big lever is batching and KV cache — you can get 30-50% token cost reduction with prefix caching.
[03:25] Tom: can you explain KV cache? we've seen that term but not exactly how it behaves at scale. sometimes cache invalidation is tricky.
[03:33] Jordan: absolutely — our KV cache holds key-value states for decoder-only models' attention states. if your app uses repeated contexts (like few-shot prompts or chat turn history), KV cache reduces recomputation. invalidation is per-session or explicit TTL, and we have controls in the console to tune TTLs and memory budgets.
[03:55] Sarah: is that the same as the 'prefix cache' you mentioned?
[03:58] Jordan: yes sometimes we call it prefix or KV cache. naming varies. we can set per-route cache rules.
[04:10] [04:10] Maya: quick aside — Optimize gives suggestions on batching settings and quantization profiles by looking at your token distribution. we'll demo Optimize in a bit.
[04:20] Ravi: cost question — if we move from openai per-token to redwood hosted pricing + caching, what's the expected unit cost delta?
[04:27] Jordan: depends on model selection. typical observed is 20-40% lower unit token cost for similar model family using caching and batching. we'll include a cost model in the parity sheet with your baseline numbers.
[04:40] Tom: any change in output determinism? we've got pipelines that rely on stable outputs for regression tests.
[04:47] Jordan: same seed/temperature behaviors; however, differences in tokenizers and small truncation heuristics can cause mismatches. we recommend a quick evaluation set to detect regressions, and Redwood's rollout tools let you do canary tests and auto-fallback to previous model variants.
[05:10] Sarah: can we do A/B by percent and monitor prompt-anchored evals?
[05:14] Jordan: yep. built-in rollouts let you assign traffic percentages, and Optimize can tie evaluations to prompt sets with regression alerts.
[05:26] [05:26] Maya: i'll show the console — jordan hop back in to demo the model route config.
[05:32] [05:32] Jordan (screen): console, top-left is Routes -> the route you create maps to a model family, default model version, and behavior policy. here we have a route called "lum-chat" that points to redwood/gptx-claude-ish (example). you can pin versions, set fallback order, and add prefetch caching.
[05:50] Sarah: where do we set headers to sign requests with our KMS-backed key?
[05:55] Jordan: under Integrations -> Keys, you can add KMS providers (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HSM). the console stores only key references. for private deployments the key material stays in your VPC.
[06:08] Tom: latency from our east coast region — do you have region routing? we don't want cross-region hops.
[06:14] Jordan: yes we support region routing and can pin your tenant to a region for hosted or place private nodes in your preferred region. Smart routing policies can fall back to other regions under capacity constraints.
[06:28] Ravi: related to that, what is SLA for hosted vs dedicated?
[06:33] Maya: hosted has best-effort with published performance profiles. Dedicated comes with committed throughput and SLA (monthly uptime and p95 latency target). Private has enterprise SLA defined in the contract.
[06:48] Sarah: anything we should know about model quantization? we want to run some 8-bit/4-bit options to reduce cost.
[06:56] Jordan: Optimize will recommend quant profiles per model + workload. we support int8 and 4-bit quant variants for many open models. there's a small accuracy delta to measure; Optimize can run a quick eval on your prompt set to show quality vs cost tradeoffs.
[07:20] [07:20] Ravi: do you guys host fine-tuned models? we have a few in-house fine-tunes on Together.
[07:26] Jordan: yes, we can serve fine-tuned artifacts in both hosted and private modes. for third-party weights we handle storage and inference; for private you can point to your artifact repo. Sally—uh sarah? sorry.
[07:40] Sarah: (laughs) no worries. what about data retention and logs? we need audit trails for compliance.
[07:47] Maya: audit logs are available in Console -> Audit, with exports to S3 or your SIEM. retention configurable per-account. for private deployments they remain within your environment.
[08:02] Tom: ok would like to see an example audit entry.
[08:06] Jordan: i'll paste a sample after the call. link to sample audit exported file: https://redwood.example/reports/sample-audit.csv (placeholder)
[08:20] [08:20] Sarah: security question — you said SOC2. is there a pen test report we can review?
[08:25] Maya: yes, we'll attach a redacted pentest artifact and SOC2 summary to the follow-up.
[08:32] Ravi: perfect. now, specific migration steps — what's typical timeline for a pilot and ramp?
[08:38] Jordan: typical pilot: 1) parity mapping + smoke tests (1 week), 2) 48-72h pilot with traffic shadowing or small percentage canary (1 week), 3) rollouts and A/B (1-2 weeks) depending on internal approvals. so 2-4 weeks overall for a conservative pilot.
[08:58] Sarah: for our case, we'd want to start with non-PHI endpoints and then test PHI in private.
[09:05] Maya: agreed that's a common path.
[09:10] [09:10] Jordan: demo time — Optimize tab now. it shows recommended batch_size, token cutoffs, and quant profiles. you can run a simulated cost estimate using your sample distribution. here's an example: baseline requests/day 200k, median length 280 tokens -> Optimize suggests batch size 8, int8 quant on the model variant, predicted 35% cost save.
[09:40] Sarah: simulation looks promising. can Optimize generate a config we can drop into our infra repo?
[09:45] Jordan: yes, there's an export as YAML/JSON for route-level overrides.
[09:50] Tom: on the infra side, do you provide a k8s operator or helm chart for private? how do we manage node pools?
[09:57] Jordan: private comes with Helm charts and operator patterns, and we can work with your SREs on node sizing. for GPU fleet we recommend a mix of A100/V100 equivalents depending on model sizes.
[10:10] Ravi: can dedicated capacity be preemptible? we want burst flexibility.
[10:15] Maya: Dedicated supports burst capacity for spikes and autoscale policies. you'll have baseline reserved compute and optional burst pools.
[10:22] [10:22] Sarah: can we see a quick end-to-end request — send from our app, go through your route, hitting cached prefix?
[10:30] Jordan (demo): sure. hitting route "lum-chat" with a 3-turn convo. watch network panel — first request cold, p95 420ms; second request with KV hit 150ms. the streaming chunks come through with the "chunk_id" fields. note the transcript framing might be slightly different than what you've seen from openai.
[10:58] Sarah: those p95 numbers look good. how reproducible are they across days?
[11:03] Jordan: we publish per-model variance and you can pin to dedicated to stabilize. also we provide token-level cost breakdown per request in console.
[11:15] Tom: what's the approach for rollback if a new model variant causes regressions?
[11:20] Jordan: automatic fallback policies: if model X breaches latency or error thresholds, traffic is rerouted to fallback model Y. you can set thresholds and notification rules.
[11:33] Ravi: great, now about the anthropic components — we use anthropic for a safety layer. can Redwood integrate existing safety tooling?
[11:41] Jordan: you can keep Anthropic as a separate step in your pipeline or we can surface safety hints as metadata. many customers keep a small gating step externally, others build in Redwood safety webhooks.
[11:55] Sarah: is there an easy way to keep both vendors during a trial — e.g., shadow traffic to Redwood but keep OpenAI/Anthropic live?
[12:02] Maya: yes — traffic mirroring is supported so you can shadow to Redwood and compare outputs without impacting production.
[12:10] [12:10] Tom: logging overhead for mirroring — is that synchronous? could it add latency?
[12:15] Jordan: mirroring is async by default, non-blocking, so production latencies are unaffected.
[12:23] Sarah: curious about cost attribution — can we see token cost per route and per team?
[12:29] Jordan: Console has cost breakdowns per-route, per-token, and by token type (prompt/response). you can also map usage to teams via token tags.
[12:40] Ravi: ok next — can you show the rollout UI for a canary?
[12:45] Jordan (screen): on the rollout page you pick base model, canary model, traffic percent (e.g., 5%), monitoring conditions (p95 latency, error rate, eval regression). there's an auto-rollback toggle.
[12:58] Sarah: auto-rollback would be ideal. do you also expose Prometheus metrics hooks?
[13:03] Jordan: yes, metrics export via metrics endpoint, and we include OpenTelemetry traces.
[13:12] Tom: does the private deployment expose the same metrics endpoints?
[13:16] Jordan: yes — same endpoints, just within your network for private mode.
[13:24] [13:24] Maya: we've been through a lot — quick check on pilot acceptance criteria? Ravi, Sarah — what would you need to call a pilot successful?
[13:32] Ravi: p95 latency within 10% of current baseline, no more than 2% regressions on our eval set, and no major ops friction.
[13:40] Sarah: plus a security signoff for the non-PHI endpoints.
[13:44] Maya: perfect. we'll bake those into the pilot plan.
[13:50] [13:50] Jordan: technical deep-dive note — for fine-tunes we recommend a small regen eval to catch tokenization differences. we'll include an example test harness.
[14:02] Tom: if we do the 48h pilot, what's the minimal integration effort? we wanted to avoid big refactors.
[14:09] Jordan: minimal path: 1) add a small adapter to target Redwood endpoints (2-3 dev days), 2) wire up shadowing/mirroring (1 day), 3) run smoke and eval harness (1-2 days).
[14:25] Sarah: do you have SDK helpers for node/python to switch between providers?
[14:30] Jordan: yes, our SDK offers a shim that maps openai-style parameters to Redwood, plus examples for anthropic/together.
[14:38] [14:38] Maya: pricing — we'll provide a quote for hosted pilot and dedicated sizing options.
[14:44] Ravi: would like to see cost delta scenarios — conservative and aggressive.
[14:48] Jordan: we'll include those in the parity spreadsheet: baseline, cached-enabled, and quant-enabled scenarios.
[14:55] Sarah: about model families — we are using Together's llama-variant for some heavy embeddings. does Redwood offer embeddings parity?
[15:02] Jordan: yes, we have embeddings endpoints and match for many open families; note that vector dimensionality sometimes differs across vendors — Optimize will reconcile and offer migration helpers.
[15:18] Tom: do you offer an embeddings reindex tool as part of migration?
[15:22] Jordan: we offer scripts and a reindex guide; for larger corpuses we can co-run a reindex job under pilot to measure timings.
[15:32] [15:32] Sarah: any gotchas about rate limits? we've hit burst throttles with OpenAI before.
[15:37] Jordan: rate limits are configurable per-tenant and per-route. rate-limiting + quota controls are in the Console and can be enforced at token or request level.
[15:48] Ravi: let's talk timeline again briefly — we aim to start a non-PHI pilot in two weeks. anything blocking from Redwood side?
[15:55] Maya: from our side, we'll prepare parity sheet, pilot test plan, SOC2 docs, and sample audit logs — these are low-friction.
[16:05] Tom: we'll collect traffic profile and provide a sample dataset.
[16:10] Maya: perfect.
[16:14] [16:14] Jordan: one more demo piece — failover config. here's a route with fallback to a smaller, cheaper model. threshold set to 10% errors triggers fallback and notifications sent to pager duty.
[16:30] Sarah: oh nice. PD integration — you support that?
[16:33] Jordan: yep, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Slack, email.
[16:38] [16:38] Maya: ok quick recap / next steps before we wrap, folks.
[16:42] Ravi: sure.
[16:44] Maya: action items: we'll send parity spreadsheet, sample audit, and pilot plan. Jordan will scope pilot and test configs. Tom will send traffic logs. we'll schedule infra deep dive next week.
[16:58] Sarah: one last question — in the console can we tag routes to teams and enforce per-team quotas?
[17:04] Jordan: yes, teams and org-level policies supported; RBAC controls who can edit routes.
[17:10] Tom: any recommended observability knobs we should enable during pilot?
[17:15] Jordan: enable token-level breakdown, request traces for sample sessions, and the regression alert on prompt sets.
[17:22] [17:22] Maya: cool. wrapping — thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the materials.
[17:28] Ravi: thanks. nice session.
[17:30] Sarah: appreciate it.
